morning everyone, on behalf of the EMRIP, I want to warmly welcome all our esteemed panelists and participants, including indigenous peoples representatives, member states, national human rights institutions, United Nations entities, academic institutions, non-governmental organizations, OHCHR indigenous fellows, Grantees and all others joining our discussion today. It's my pleasure to chair this timely and very important panel on the rights of indigenous peoples and artificial intelligence. As artificial intelligence rapidly transforms societies across the world, it's essential that discussions on these technologies fully incorporate the rights, perspectives and priorities of indigenous peoples. AI presents significant opportunities, including for the revitalisation of indigenous languages, the preservation of oral histories and knowledge systems, and the transmission of cultural heritage to future generations. At the same time, it raises profound concerns, including algorithmic bias, misrepresentation of indigenous knowledge systems and perspectives, exclusion from decision-making processes, the extraction and use of indigenous peoples' data without their free prior informed consent, and the use of AI-enabled surveillance and profiling practices that may disproportionately affect indigenous peoples. Moreover, these developments risk creating new forms of digital inequality, colonialism, technological exploitation and dispossession that can undermine indigenous people's self-determination and data sovereignty. These challenges underscore the need to ensure that AI governance frameworks are firmly grounded in international human rights standards, particularly the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. The central message of today's panel is clear. The future of AI must be shaped in a way that respects, protects and fulfills the rights of indigenous peoples. This includes recognition of indigenous data governance principles and indigenous peoples authority over data concerning their communities, cultures, territories and knowledge systems. It requires respect for the rights to self-determination, meaningful participation in decision-making, free, prior, and informed consent, as well as control over cultural heritage, traditional knowledge, and indigenous data sovereignty. These principles must guide the development, deployment, and governance of AI technologies and inform efforts to advance inclusive, ethical, and rights-based approaches to AI. At the same time, we are witnessing the growing leadership of indigenous peoples in the area of data governance and digital innovation across regions. Indigenous led initiatives are demonstrating how technology, including AI, can be developed and used in ways that strengthen languages, protect knowledge systems, support responsible stewardship of lands and resources and advance collective well-being. These experiences remind us that indigenous peoples are not only rights holders whose interests must be protected. They are also innovators and partners in shaping ethical, inclusive and sustainable technological futures. This today's panel provides an opportunity to examine the implications of AI for indigenous peoples, highlight indigenous led good practices and identify pathways to ensure that emerging technologies are governed in a manner consistent with the UN declaration on the rights of indigenous peoples. The outcomes of today's discussion, including its key recommendations, will inform the expert mechanisms annual report to the Human Rights Council. As we begin our discussion, I encourage our panelists to propose actionable recommendations for states, indigenous peoples, United Nations entities, and other stakeholders to support rights-based and inclusive AI governance. Today's panel brings together indigenous experts, rights holders, policy makers, and technical practitioners. We have six distinguished speakers with us, each bringing a wealth of experience, knowledge, and insight into this important discussion. We're honored that you've accepted our invitation and taken the time to join us today And I want to thank you and give you a warm welcome once again. And I will start now by giving the floor to Maren Nystad Storset representing the Sami Parliament in Norway. Madam Storset is a member of the Sami Parliament's Executive Council and a Sami politician representing the Norwegian Sami National Association. She has professional experience in indigenous governance and policy development within the Sapmi region. Her areas of expertise include protecting developing Sami languages as well as digitalization and artificial intelligence. Madam Storslett, you have seven minutes.

Chair, distinguished members of the Expert Mechanism, colleagues and fellow indigenous peoples, I would like to thank the Expert Mechanism for the invitation to contribute to this important and highly relevant panel. The rapid development of artificial intelligence is transforming our society beyond what we can imagine. For indigenous peoples, this brings both significant opportunities and serious risks. For instance, in areas where human resources with language expertise are limited, AI can serve as a vital tool to ensure our languages remain accessible. AI can also strengthen public services, healthcare, education, and access to justice. It can also offer vital opportunities for development within traditional livelihoods, cultural heritage and traditions. Today, however, indigenous peoples remain largely underrepresented in national, regional and international processes shaping AI regulations, standards and ethical frameworks. Indigenous peoples must take a leading role in discussions on AI at all levels. including within the UN, with a human rights-based approach, grounded firmly in the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, particularly the right to self-determination, participation, and the free, prior, and informed consent. And I warmly welcome the expert mechanism's timely focus on this issue. Chair, in Norway, the government has launched a national AI initiative. For the Sami Parliament, it is crucial to ensure that we are included in these national efforts, so that new language models reflect our realities and benefits our communities. We also see an important role of strengthening collaboration with regional processes, for instance, within the European Union and its institutions. to ensure that emerging frameworks do not become restricted barriers, but instead incorporate safeguards for indigenous rights and self-determination. In Sami, we have the Sami AI lab at the Sami University of Applied Sciences. They have already developed vital tools for the Sami community despite limited funding. Capacity building and support of indigenous led centers of expertise and institutions is highly important to ensure our meaningful participation and capacity on these matters. We also need to strengthen cooperation among indigenous peoples on AI. We must build alliances and networks between indigenous experts and institutions to exchange best practice, address shared challenges, and co-develop AI systems. With adequate resources and clear mandates, these institutions can drive technological development on our own terms and in accordance with our priorities. They serve to steward and quality assure AI systems being deployed, preventing misrepresentation, algorithm bias, and further marginalization. As AI systems increasingly depend on large-scale data collection, and many AI models are trained on data collected from open sources, Indigenous peoples must have real influence over how data relating to our languages, culture, people, society and knowledge systems are collected, governed and used. Data sovereignty and indigenous data governance is a natural extension of the right to self-determination. Also, algorithm bias within AI systems may produce stereotypical and harmful representation in AI-generated outputs. If AI models are not trained on accurate or representative data, they fail to understand our realities. In critical sectors like healthcare, this can result in unreliable tools that provide wrong health assessments. The concentration of technological power within a few global corporate actors also raise critical questions about whose values and priorities are embedded in these AI systems. Just as we have ethical standards and corporate responsibility frameworks in other major industries, we strongly suggest that something similar should be expected from the tech industry. Furthermore, we must not only ask what AI can do, but what it should do. AI is resource intensive and requires vast amounts of energy. In Sami, we already see how large data centers put immersive pressure on our territories. And mining activities related to this development of these data centers threatens indigenous peoples' lands. This comes on top of other extractive activities, and this forces a conversation about priorities and limits, and we need to be at the table on these discussions. Chair, respect for the rights of indigenous peoples must apply across the entire life of AI systems. This includes the fundamental principles of free, prior, and informed consent. We must ensure indigenous peoples' participation in decision making, the governance of indigenous data and knowledge, and promote forms for technological development that strengthen our communities. And I would encourage the EMRIP to consider studies and recommendations on the implementation of UNDRIP in the age of AI, ensuring that AI becomes a tool for empowerment, not further marginalization. so that we are on the forefront of this development. Chair, I look forward to hear other inputs on this agenda today.

Thank you very much, Madam Storset. Now I'd like to give the floor to Emily Pugin, High Commissioner to Cyprus, former director in Australia's Office for First Nations international engagement. She's a proud Kombumerri First Nations woman and has served overseas at the Australian Embassy and the permanent mission to the United Nations in Vienna and Austria. Madam Pujin, you have seven minutes.

Thank you, Chair, and colleagues, which means good morning in the Kombumerri dialect. I would like to begin by thanking the expert mechanism for its leadership in advancing the rights of indigenous peoples as digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, rapidly reshape societies, economies and public decision making. This is a timely and important discussion. For Australia, the central question is not whether AI will affect indigenous peoples, but whether it is developed and governed with indigenous peoples. in accordance with their rights, priorities and knowledge systems. AI can be a powerful tool for opportunity and inclusion when it is shaped by the people and communities that it affects. However, without effective governance, it can also deepen exclusion, reproduce bias, misuse data and undermine cultural identity. Australia strongly supports a human rights based approach to AI governance and in the context of Indigenous peoples, this is guided by three priorities. Rights based governance, Indigenous data sovereignty and meaningful participation. These priorities are underpinned by safeguards, Indigenous led opportunity, partnership and international cooperation. AI governance should be grounded in human rights and the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, guided by self-determination, participation in decision-making, free, prior and informed consent, and protection of cultural heritage. Indigenous peoples must be active partners and decision-makers in how systems are designed, used, assessed, and governed through the lifecycle of AI. Indigenous data sovereignty must also be central to human rights respecting AI. Indigenous peoples have the right to govern the collection, ownership, access, interpretation and use of data relating to their communities, lands, cultures, languages and knowledge systems. In AI systems, data shapes design, training, outputs and the assumptions embedded in automated tools. Respecting Indigenous data sovereignty is essential to ensuring that AI systems are accurate, culturally appropriate, accountable and trusted. Australia recognises the importance of strengthening data sovereignty so that First Nations communities retain appropriate control over how their data is accessed and used. Meaningful participation must be enabled through targeted safeguards, digital inclusion and Indigenous-led opportunity. AI can create real opportunities for Indigenous communities when it is designed, deployed and governed responsibly. When Indigenous peoples lead innovation, AI and digital tools can support language revitalisation, cultural preservation, land and sea management, environmental monitoring, service access and economic participation. However, there are also risks to Indigenous peoples. These include algorithmic bias, harmful stereotyping, misappropriation of cultural and intellectual property, use of data without proper consent, and outputs that fail to reflect cultural context, language diversity, or community authority. Addressing these risks is critical to building trust and ensuring that innovation does not come at the expense of rights. As such, Australia supports safeguards that are transparent, accountable, culturally informed, with stronger protections for cultural knowledge and clearer redress where harm occurs. Technology should strengthen, not replace, Indigenous knowledge systems, with communities defining the problem, shaping the solution and governing the outcomes. Participation also requires practical action to address digital exclusion, which risks compounding existing inequalities as AI becomes more embedded across economies and societies. Australia is working to address this through digital inclusion, connectivity, skills development, AI literacy and community led initiatives so that Indigenous peoples are protected from harm and empowered to participate in and benefit from the digital economy. Australia's Department of Industry, Science and Resources is leading national work on responsible AI. This includes whole of government policy engagement focused on safe, inclusive and human rights respecting approaches. Australia's national action plan continues to build on our robust legal and regulatory framework and AI ethics principles are designed to capture opportunity, spread benefits and ensure the responsible design, development and use of AI systems. These principles support Australia's efforts to harness the potential of AI safely and responsibly. Australia will also establish the Australian AI Safety Institute to monitor and test AI systems, provide timely insights on emerging risks and support fit for purpose protections that keep pace with technological change. The Australian Government is also committed to legislating a digital duty of care to the Online Safety Act, which will require online service providers to undertake thorough and regular risk assessments and implement effective mitigation strategies to address new and emerging AI-related risks and harms. Across these priorities, partnership is fundamental. Australia emphasises sustained engagement so that Indigenous peoples help shape AI governance frameworks, safeguards, policies and programs, including through co-design and support for Indigenous-led solutions that reflect local priorities and cultural authority. Effective AI governance at all levels requires that First Nations communities have a meaningful voice in shaping their digital future. not only through access to technology, but also through sharing in the benefits that it creates. Effective governance cannot be developed for Indigenous peoples without their perspectives, knowledge and leadership. In closing, Chair, international cooperation is critical. AI is a global technology and its challenges cannot be addressed by any one country alone. Australia is committed to working with partners to promote inclusive AI governance, share approaches to Indigenous data governance, and ensure global standards reflect diversity, cultural context, and human rights. Forums such as EMRIP have an important role in ensuring Indigenous perspectives are reflected in global discussions on AI. Australia reaffirms its commitment to digital transformation that is safe, inclusive, human rights respecting, and empowering for Indigenous peoples. The measure of responsible AI will be whether it is developed with Indigenous peoples, respects their rights and knowledge, and delivers benefits defined by their communities. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Madam Chair. Good morning, colleagues, experts. Thank you to the EMRIP for the invitation allowing me to speak on such a crucial theme. AI is an instrument which can provide benefits, but it can do good, but it can also pose threats to indigenous peoples, AI opens for indigenous peoples broad opportunities for revitalizing languages, economic development, preserving traditional knowledge, environmental monitoring. However, at the same time, AI systems raise new kinds of ethical problems, illegitimate use of traditional knowledge, blurring the identities of indigenous peoples, AI systems can also heighten the negative prejudices and worsen existing forms of stereotypes and prejudices towards indigenous peoples. The goal today is to find a model where AI technologies can serve the interests of indigenous peoples and not the other way around. Currently, in many countries, there's active development of legislative regulation of AI, but approaches vary significantly. In Russia, AI legislation is still developing. In Russia, there is a national AI development strategy running up to 2030 that was approved by presidential decree last week in the Russian parliament. There was adoption of a bill on AI legal regulation about developing framework approaches to AI development. That document regulates issues of lawful use of the results of intellectual activities. One of the norms contained is to mark all audiovisual materials created with the help of neural networks. This helps protect from hidden manipulation and discriminatory algorithms. Colleagues, as part of today's discussion, I want to draw your attention to collective study that was developed by organisations of indigenous peoples of Russia. in support of an EMRIP survey on the right to data. It's called Indigenous Peoples Disaggregated Data and Access to Information. That study highlights practices and priorities for indigenous peoples in Russia when it comes to digitalization, including in the sphere of AI. languages are a key area where AI opens significant opportunities for indigenous peoples in Russia I'll give you a few examples from our socio-cultural region in Russia you have a project called languages of the peoples of Russia it's implemented by the IT company Yandex together with the organization the home of Russian peoples with the support of the federal agency on nationalities 21 indigenous languages already accessible on Yandex. Six languages are available for word recognition and synthesis. In other words, it helps neural nets analyze sound patterns and transform them into words and also analyze text and then place a human voice with the language of the indigenous language. The plan is that very soon 25 indigenous languages will be available on those services. Now, of course, similar projects and initiatives on digitalization of languages have already been implemented several years ago in a number of countries, but what's interesting is that in Russia such initiatives have become a priority. for state linguistic policy and have been implemented systemically given the large number of languages in Russia. According to experts, there's probably around 270 languages plus dialects. Now separately, I'd like to stress the importance of participation of indigenous peoples themselves in this process. For example, in Sakha Yakutia Republic, at the initiative of indigenous organizations, there's implementation of a project digitalization of linguistic and cultural heritage of the Arctic indigenous peoples. In Krasnoyarsk, with the support of regional associations, we're developing a project with a system of AI called Smart Chom. That's the name, Smart Chom. And this is to help herders using internet and with a satellite connection and then the person can monitor herding and using a drone quadcopter he can monitor direction of deer, use services of telemedicine, etc. Another example I'd like to draw your attention to was recently presented by linguistic activists during the third international summit World Treasures of Native Languages recently. It's an extension for the EthnoTech browser, which automatically translates voice and video tracks into indigenous languages using AI. It allows immediately, without dubbing, to maintain the voice intonation and watch videos in the native language. of indigenous languages. Currently this can be done in 15 languages including in Mordov, Mokshans, Erzyans, in Votsk language, that's one of the small number indigenous peoples. Now these examples are to be welcomed and supported. We should point out that for practical embodiment of such ideas significant investment is required and a relevant level of expertise. Colleagues, I'd like to draw your attention also that the fact that AI is a sphere of international competition, AI development has heightened competition between states, between companies, at the same time in many developing countries there's… an absence of relevant infrastructure, there's not so much in the way of technical opportunities and or investment that's needed for to benefit from and implement AI. Such countries therefore often depend on technologies from outside. Separately, there's the need to remove artificial barriers that hinder access for indigenous peoples to new technologies, to protecting their sovereignty and their intellectual property rights. Unfortunately, what we see is that use unilateral coercive measures can be used as levers of economic and political pressure. Indigenous organizations in Russia have repeatedly stated at UN fora and called on mandate holders to develop guiding principles of due diligence to prevent or minimize harm to indigenous peoples. In conclusion, I'd like to call on UN mechanisms specialized agencies in the UN system to develop an international document. This could be a strategy or a global plan of action that would take into account the rights of indigenous peoples when using AI technologies and also to develop a mechanism for a complaints mechanism for violations of rights using AI. Undoubtedly, strict ethical regulation is required to avoid illegitimate use of the sensitive knowledge of indigenous peoples. And a starting point here could be the ethical principles of AI use that were developed by UNESCO back in 2021. Colleagues, AI is not just a technology, it's a reflection of our own values. If we want to build a fair, just future, we need to guarantee that AI can develop inclusively, ethically, respecting the rights and interests of indigenous peoples. I thank you.

Thank you very much for that statement. Next, I would like to invite Noelani Arista, director of Institute for Indigenous Research and Knowledge, Faculty of Arts at McGill University. Ms. Arista is an indigenous historian of Hawaii, an expert on the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning to support indigenous language sources and to increase community access to Aike Hawaii through indigenous centered approaches to knowledge organization. Madam Arista, you have the floor, seven minutes.

Thank you. Aloha mai kakou. Aloha to the indigenous people of this land and from around the world. Mahalo to the members of the expert mechanism for the invitation to contribute to this important discussion on artificial intelligence and its impacts on indigenous communities. I have 25 years of training and experience in Hawaiian language historical research, as well as textual and archival organization of primary sources from Hawaii, arguably the largest indigenous language textual archive in native North America and the Moananuiakea. My training with native speakers was kinesthetic, aural, and oral. And our elders taught us that the greatest threat to our knowledges was forgetting, but they could not foresee the digital present. Inundated as we are by a world of words, sound bites, images, and video snippets rendered through social media and generated by AI. At present, the greatest threat to indigenous knowledges is distortion and the session of community control to digital mediums. The term data sovereignty is often used. I have heard it in multinational indigenous projects I work with, but there is little agreement on what the term means, much less the mechanisms or processes that should be codified to ensure that indigenous knowledges are protected and persist for our futurity. In my work, I have been asked to organize archival collections for greater access, build standalone digital repositories that are open sourced. and have consulted on Indigenous community projects regarding best practices for AI integration into the management of sensitive community data sets. A singular challenge is that there are no local, regional, or governmental organizations tasked with reaching out and providing education for Indigenous communities on the promise and possible dangers of AI and data organization. Here, I would highlight the first of several challenges to traditional knowledge systems. the transformation of TKS into data. How do we best mobilize machine learning and AI applications to support the social relations governed by behavioral norms and community-based ethical standards that transcend a single generation? For most of us, knowledge is not data. Its foremost use is not extraction for wealth generation. It is neither alienable nor property. Put simply, how do we preserve correct knowledge and create supports through AI that do not sacrifice live relations or violate or devalue longstanding ethical norms and protocols? How do we do so while protecting our lands and waters? Do we or anyone else on the planet have a right to refusal? At present, there are many initiatives to use AI for language reclamation. In my experience, however, many of these teams are led by computer scientists and linguists with few fluent language speakers or traditional knowledge experts shaping the trajectory of work. While governments promote optimistic plans promising AI for all, there are few indigenous people at the table who are trained in both computer science and indigenous knowledges and languages, necessitating conscientious and respectful collaboration. Our current AI boom has the energy of a nascent gold rush, and the people who supply funds or technological savvy are the ones who drive decision making, content creation, and delivery. Far too often, project leaders are unfamiliar with our languages, the cultural protocols governing the care and transmission of knowledge, and have not considered the socially corrosive effects of new technologies. Due diligence must be pursued to understand people's credentials and authority so that identity doesn't supplant IK or traditional knowledge and community protocols and expertise are honored. Two years ago, my colleagues and I started an indigenous language revitalization program at McGill University, granting both masters and doctoral degrees, as well as an iterative lab where students from history, law, linguistics, and library and computer science may collaborate on various research projects that are dedicated to bringing language and knowledge back to communities. Here, language is not treated as an isolate, but rather as an integral part of putting people back into good relations with one another and giving life to healthy communities. So far, student-led collaborative projects include a digital dictionary co-created with elders in the Swampy Cree dialect, producing machine-read scans of Maori language newspapers, and new standards for language vitality in Ganienkehaga communities. Upcoming projects will map traditional place names, gather historical and contemporary land stewardship practices, and monitor land and environmental transformation over time. We are working collaboratively with students and professors to monitor the legal landscape with respect to our rights and protections. While there are cases wherein a government chooses adoption of the stricter UNDRIP standards into their domestic legislation. Canada nor the United States has a centralized indigenous data sovereignty regulatory framework. In the absence of formal legislation, nonprofit organizations and other interest groups have filled the gap, creating several indigenous data privacy standards that establish more indigenous specific norms to govern research conducted on indigenous communities. While some, sorry, of these standards are recognized and supported by the respective federal governments for internal purposes, they are not formal legislation and therefore not strictly binding. Rather, the intent is setting norms that support Indigenous data sovereignty within government agencies, research spaces, and other third-party organizations. As these standards are guidelines rather than protections with the backing of law, indigenous stewardship control access and possession of traditional knowledge systems remains at risk from the highly competitive, fast moving and unfettered development and implementation of AI systems globally. Therefore, in accord with Article 13 of the UN Declaration of Rights on Indigenous Peoples on the right to revitalize, use, develop and transmit to future generations our languages, oral traditions, writing systems and literatures, and Article 14 and 16 on our right to establish educational systems and media in our languages, we call on international bodies and EMRIP to recognize indigenous expertise and ability to contribute to the development of ethical AI systems and to apply pressure to individual nations to more strongly regulate the entities within and between their jurisdictions in the interest of meaningful protection of indigenous rights in AI development. and the protection of indigenous peoples' lands, seas, and waters.

Thank you very much for that statement. I'd like to invite Olivier Alias, program coordinator at the United Nations International Telecommunication Union. Mr. Alias has worked on integrating human rights considerations into digital governance and technical standards with a focus on artificial intelligence and inclusive digital transformation. Madam Chairperson, distinguished experts, excellencies, dear colleagues, thank you very much for having invited me to speak on behalf of the International Telecommunications Union. This is the United Nations specialized agency for digital technologies. Today I'd like to develop three points. Connectivity is not yet a right that has fully been acquired by indigenous peoples. Artificial intelligence may either exacerbate that exclusion or contribute to remedying it, depending on how it's conceived. And technical standards, these rules which are largely invisible but which determine the behaviour of technologies, are a legitimate and thus far underexploited space for indigenous participation. Let me turn first of all to connectivity then. Today, 2.2 billion people remain unconnected. Indigenous peoples, over 476 million individuals over some 90 countries with around 5,000 different cultures and languages are structurally overrepresented in this in this non-connectivity. This isn't mere geographical chance. This is a reflection of ancient, old, longstanding patterns of dispossession, removal, and investment in infrastructure which have constantly bypassed indigenous territories where connectivity is lacking. We also see a lack of more recent digital economy tools such as cloud services, AI, and harmonisation and alignment bodies that discreetly shape those technologies. That is why the ITU is supporting connectivity headed by indigenous peoples themselves, and not just connectivity that is delivered to indigenous communities. That is a commitment that our member states have formally mandated for over two decades now, and it was recently reaffirmed in resolution 46, which was adopted last year at the World Telecommunications Development Conference in Baku. That resolution was also based on resolution 184 adopted by our Plenipot conference in 2022 a training program that we've been carrying out with Regional Partners in 19 countries in Latin America have enabled the NASA uh Garifuna, Quechua, Wich, Digar, Kuti, Kalchaki and Guarani communities to build exploit and maintain their own networks around 120 um uh individuals, including four out of 10 are women, have then trained thousands of other people. The lesson that we are learning, and this is the first question, really, is not just to know whether a community is connected, but under what conditions it is connected. Let me turn more now to AI. This is increasingly relevant here. AI systems are largely trained on a handful of dominant languages, and the assessments presented this year at the WISYS forum suggest that up to four billion people whose mother tongues, cultures and local knowledge remain underrepresented in the training data would get very unreliable results or distorted results from AI systems that are now incorporated into public services, into education and to daily search engines. For indigenous languages, many of them already threatened after decades of active suppression. And this is not just a simple technical precision problem, it's additional pressure and it's more silent pressure towards deletion. However, this same technology under indigenous control can produce the opposite effect in New Zealand. Tehiku Media have developed an AI tool aiming to collect and preserve oral recordings in Te Reo Maori, and they've placed that recently collected data under a license which is, which is held, the governance of which is held within the community and expressly prohibits its use for the purposes of surveillance or discrimination. As one of the designers said, data is the new earth and people who have seen territorial disposition understand exactly why data sovereignty is not something that needs to be thought about as a secondary issue. This model needs to be further widespread, not just AI applied to indigenous peoples, but AI governed by them on infrastructure and according to licensing conditions that they control. The ITU resolution on multilingualism commits our members to supporting linguistic diversity in ICTs and the task now is to expand this commitment in the era of AI. Let me turn now to my third point and that's technical standards. Member States of the ITU adopted at our last global assembly on telecommunications in 2024 a resolution on our standards work in AI regarding reliability and our members are currently looking at simple guidelines which are human focused, aiming at identifying from the beginning of the process of drafting standards risks linked to human rights before the systems are built rather than after they've caused harm. And it is precisely at that point that the sovereignty of indigenous data, linguistic rights and language rights and the principle of free prior informed consent must be incorporated into the choices of technical concepts and not just added in years later following a dispute or as part of a policy. Indigenous peoples have their place in this room and in that room within the study commissions of the ITU and in the broader ensemble of the AI governance process, which is building and being shaped in, for example, in the first UN global dialogue on AI governance that was held in Geneva last week. Madam Chair, the ITU isn't claiming to speak on behalf of indigenous peoples, but we are committed to working on three specific elements, continuing to work with community networks conducted by indigenous peoples, supporting AI in the service of common good, which includes indigenous communities, and encouraging indigenous participation in our digital technical standards processes in line with applicable provisions governing the members of the ITU. Technology is not at the heart of injustices. experienced by indigenous peoples, but if it is devised without caution, it can exacerbate them. If built within a genuine spirit of partnership, it can help indigenous peoples to do what they've always done to preserve their languages, their knowledge and their self-determination in their own conditions.

Assalamu alaikum, distinguished members of EMRIP, colleagues and participants. It is an honor to join you today on behalf of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions, or GANHRI. We thank the expert mechanism for the invitation to contribute to this important discussion in indigenous peoples and artificial intelligence. Artificial intelligence is already shaping decisions that affect indigenous peoples' lives in profound ways. from access to public services, land and environmental management, health diagnostics, education tools, to policing and border governance. Yet the systems are often developed without the meaningful participation of indigenous peoples, and in many cases without adequate safeguards to protect their rights, data, and knowledge systems. From a human rights perspective, this raises both urgent concerns and important possibilities. On the one hand, we are witnessing well-documented risks. First, algorithmic bias and discrimination. AI systems are frequently trained on data sets and underrepresent or misrepresent Indigenous peoples, their languages, identities, and realities. This can result in exclusion from services, distorted decision-making, or discriminatory profiling. In some contexts, automated systems reinforce historical inequalities rather than correcting them. This growing use of facial recognition technologies further illustrate this risks. Second, data sovereignty and lack of control over indigenous knowledge. AI development often involves large scale data extraction, including cultural, linguistic, environmental and even sacred knowledge. Without free, prior and informed consent, this can amount to a form of digital dispossession where indigenous peoples lose control over how their knowledge is used, stored and monetized. Third, Surveillance and misuse of technologies. AI-powered surveillance tools, including facial recognition and predictive analytics, have in some cases been used in ways that disproportionately affect indigenous communities, particularly in context of land defense and environmental protection. For example, the Australian Human Rights Commission has highlighted concerns regarding the use of emerging AI-enabled policing and criminal justice technologies, including the deployment of real-time facial recognition technologies and proactive policing tools involving drones and smart tracking in areas with significant Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations. The Commission has also raised concerns about AI-driven security risk assessment tools used in places of detention, which may classify individuals according to perceived risks of escape or violence. Fourth, digital exclusion and inequality of participation. Many indigenous communities continue to face structural barriers to digital access, infrastructure, and capacity. This means they are often absent from the design, governance and oversight of AI systems that nonetheless affect them directly. In the Philippines, for example, indigenous peoples have expressed that they find it challenging to access technology not only due to lack of connectivity, but also due to the lack of knowledge and technological use. The growing reliance of social and knowledge systems in AI and digital access has also impacted the transfer and exercise of indigenous knowledge and practices as existing indigenous systems are not digital to begin with. Fourth, the expansion of artificial intelligence carries significant environmental costs. The data centers and infrastructures required to develop and operate AI systems consume substantial amounts of energy, water, and land. In the context In the context of climate and environmental crisis, the rapid growth of AI may exacerbate existing pressures on ecosystems and natural resources. These impacts can be particularly significant for indigenous peoples whose lands and territories are often affected by large scale infrastructure project, resource extraction and environmental degradation. The Australian Human Rights Commission has also drawn attention to proposed AI data centers that may place additional pressure on indigenous lands and water resources, raising concerns about what has been described as the digital colonization of land and natural resources where indigenous peoples are not meaningfully consulted or able to exercise free, prior and informed consent. At the same time, Ganri believes it is important not to view AI only through the lens of risk. We are already seeing examples where AI and digital tools are being used to support indigenous languages revitalization, including through translation models, voice recognition tools, and digital archives co-developed with indigenous communities. There is also growing potential for AI to improve access to public services, including health diagnostics in remote areas, early warning systems for climate related risks, and educational tools adapted to local languages and contexts. The question, therefore, is not whether AI should be used in relation to indigenous peoples, but rather how it is governed, who controls it, and whose values it reflects.
